Written reports on ML Monitor Vitals
A Computer-Vision and Machine-Learning Prototype for Extraction, Verification, and Temporal Analysis of Physiological Vital Signs from Patient Monitor Images Technical prototype report
Abstract
Background

Patient monitors display multiple physiological measurements simultaneously, including heart rate, peripheral oxygen saturation, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and end-tidal carbon dioxide. Although these measurements are readily available on bedside monitoring equipment, transferring them into a digital record can require manual transcription. Optical character recognition (OCR) provides a potential mechanism for converting monitor photographs into structured physiological data.

Objective

This paper describes the design and implementation of an educational software prototype that uses computer vision, OCR, rule-based parsing, user verification, temporal visualization, and a machine-learning trend model to transform photographs of physiological monitors into structured vital-sign observations.

Methods

The application was implemented in Python using Streamlit for the interactive web interface, Pillow for image processing, regular expressions for structured blood-pressure extraction, Pandas for tabular data management, and Plotly for temporal visualization. The processing pipeline consists of five principal stages: image acquisition, OCR-based text extraction, physiological-value parsing, human verification, and longitudinal trend analysis. A specialized blood-pressure extraction pathway supplements general OCR because systolic and diastolic pressure are commonly represented as a paired numerical expression. Extracted measurements are assigned OCR-derived confidence values when available. Verified measurements are timestamped and stored in application session state. After at least three verified observations, a machine-learning model is invoked to estimate whether the recorded trajectory is improving, stable, or worsening. Rule-based clinical reference patterns are additionally generated from selected physiological thresholds.

Results

The implemented prototype provides an end-to-end workflow from monitor-image upload to structured vital-sign display, manual verification, longitudinal tabulation, visualization, and prototype trend classification. The system supports heart rate, SpO₂, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, respiratory rate, and end-tidal carbon dioxide. It also exposes OCR confidence information and provides rule-based reference considerations for selected abnormal physiological patterns.

Conclusions

The software demonstrates the feasibility of combining OCR, structured parsing, human verification, visualization, and machine-learning methods within a lightweight clinical-data interface. However, the implementation should be regarded strictly as a research and educational prototype. OCR errors, image quality limitations, parser assumptions, limited training data, absence of clinical validation, and potential distribution shift prevent the system from being interpreted as an autonomous clinical decision-support or diagnostic system.

Keywords: optical character recognition, computer vision, vital signs, physiological monitoring, machine learning, clinical informatics, human-in-the-loop systems, medical imaging, Streamlit

1. Introduction

Physiological monitoring is fundamental to the assessment of patients in emergency, prehospital, perioperative, and critical-care environments. Modern patient monitors commonly display several physiological variables simultaneously, including heart rate (HR), peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂), non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP), respiratory rate (RR), and end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO₂).

Despite the availability of these measurements in digital monitoring systems, photographs or screenshots of monitor displays are sometimes used for documentation, education, retrospective analysis, and software prototyping. Converting such images into structured data presents a computer-vision problem because the measurements are embedded within a graphical user interface rather than provided as machine-readable numerical data.

Optical character recognition provides a general mechanism for extracting textual and numerical information from images. However, physiological monitor displays introduce additional challenges. Multiple numerical values may be present simultaneously, labels may be separated spatially from their associated values, characters may be distorted by image perspective or illumination, and measurement formats may vary between manufacturers and device models.

The prototype described in this paper was designed to investigate a human-in-the-loop workflow in which OCR initially extracts candidate values, software parsing converts those candidates into structured physiological variables, and a human operator verifies the measurements before they are incorporated into a longitudinal timeline.

The architecture additionally incorporates temporal visualization and a machine-learning component intended to characterize the direction of recorded physiological trajectories. A rule-based reference layer provides contextual information regarding selected physiological patterns.

The primary design principle is therefore not autonomous interpretation, but automated extraction followed by human verification.

2. System Objectives

The prototype was developed around six functional objectives:

  • Accept a photograph of a physiological monitor.
  • Extract visible numerical information using OCR.
  • Convert OCR output into structured vital-sign variables.
  • Provide confidence information and allow manual verification.
  • Store verified observations as a time-indexed sequence.
  • Analyze and visualize temporal trends using statistical, rule-based, and machine-learning components.

The system was deliberately structured so that OCR-derived values were not automatically treated as verified clinical observations.

3. System Architecture

The application follows a modular architecture consisting of an interface layer, image-processing layer, parsing layer, state-management layer, visualization layer, and analytical layer.

The high-level processing sequence is:

Monitor Photograph

│

▼

Image Upload

│

▼

Image Preprocessing / OCR

│

├───────────────┐

▼ ▼

General OCR BP-specific OCR

│ │

▼ ▼

Vital Parser BP Candidate Filter

│ │

└───────┬───────┘

▼

Structured Vital Signs

│

▼

OCR Confidence Display

│

▼

Human Verification

│

▼

Timestamped History

│

┌───────┴────────┐

▼ ▼

Visualization ML Trend Model

│ │

└───────┬────────┘

▼

Reference Considerations

This architecture establishes a separation between extraction and interpretation. The extraction subsystem attempts to recover numerical information, whereas the user remains responsible for confirming that the extracted values correspond to the source monitor.

4. Software Environment

The prototype was implemented in Python.

The principal dependencies visible in the application include:

ComponentFunction
PythonCore programming language
StreamlitInteractive web application framework
PillowLoading and conversion of monitor images
PandasTabular data representation and timeline management
PlotlyInteractive physiological trend visualization
Regular expressionsNumerical pattern recognition, particularly blood pressure
src.ocrApplication-specific OCR functions
src.parserApplication-specific physiological-value parsing
src.mlMachine-learning trend model

The application imports three primary custom modules:

from src.ocr import extract_text, extract_bp_candidates

from src.parser import parse_vitals

and, when sufficient historical observations exist:

from src.ml import train_trend_model, predict_trend

This modular organization allows OCR, parsing, and machine-learning components to be developed independently of the graphical user interface.

5. Image Acquisition

The first stage of the workflow is image acquisition.

The interface uses Streamlit's file-upload functionality to accept JPEG and PNG images:

uploaded = st.file_uploader(

"Upload a monitor photograph",

type=["jpg", "jpeg", "png"]

)

When an image is supplied, Pillow loads the image and explicitly converts it to RGB:

image = Image.open(

uploaded

).convert("RGB")

This normalization ensures that downstream processing receives a consistent three-channel representation regardless of the original image mode.

The uploaded image is subsequently rendered within the interface so that the operator can visually inspect the source material.

6. Optical Character Recognition
6.1 General OCR

After the operator activates the monitor-reading operation, the image is passed to the general OCR subsystem:

ocr_results = extract_text(image)

The application expects the OCR subsystem to return a list of structured objects. Each object is expected to contain at least a textual representation and an associated confidence value.

Conceptually, the OCR output can be represented as:

[

{

"text": "...",

"confidence": ...

},

...

]

The application includes defensive validation:

if not isinstance(ocr_results, list):

ocr_results = []

This prevents an unexpected OCR return type from propagating directly into later stages of the application.

The OCR results are retained in application session state:

st.session_state.ocr = ocr_results

This allows the extracted text and confidence values to remain accessible after the Streamlit application reruns.

7. Physiological Value Parsing

Following OCR extraction, the recognized text is passed to a dedicated parsing function:

vitals = parse_vitals(ocr_results)

The parser converts unstructured OCR output into a structured dictionary.

The expected variables include:

  • HR
  • SpO₂
  • systolic blood pressure
  • diastolic blood pressure
  • RR
  • EtCO₂

The parser is also treated defensively:

if not isinstance(vitals, dict):

vitals = {}

This establishes a clear boundary between the OCR subsystem and the user interface.

A conceptual representation of the resulting object is:

{

"hr": ...,

"spo2": ...,

"bp_sys": ...,

"bp_dia": ...,

"rr": ...,

"etco2": ...

}

The exact implementation of parse_vitals() is contained in the external parser module and therefore cannot be inferred completely from the provided interface code. Consequently, this manuscript describes the observable interface contract rather than assuming a specific internal parsing algorithm.

8. Specialized Blood-Pressure Extraction

Blood pressure receives an additional processing pathway.

This design is important because blood pressure is represented as a paired measurement rather than a single numerical value. The prototype therefore calls:

bp_results = extract_bp_candidates(image)

Candidate text is subsequently examined using a regular expression:

r"(\d{2,3})\s*[/\-]\s*(\d{2,3})"

This expression recognizes patterns such as:

120/80

120 - 80

The extracted components are interpreted as systolic and diastolic pressure.

The prototype then applies physiological plausibility constraints:

50 <= systolic <= 250

20 <= diastolic <= 150

systolic > diastolic

Candidates failing these criteria are discarded.

If multiple valid candidates are detected, the candidate with the highest OCR confidence is selected.

This creates a simple confidence-based candidate-selection mechanism:

Candidate BP values

│

▼

Regex pattern matching

│

▼

Numerical validation

│

▼

Plausible candidates

│

▼

Highest OCR confidence

│

▼

Selected BP

The resulting blood-pressure values are then inserted into the structured vital-sign dictionary.

9. Confidence Estimation

The application incorporates a confidence-display mechanism to communicate uncertainty associated with OCR extraction.

The find_confidence() function first searches for a parser-provided confidence value:

parser_confidence = vitals.get(

f"{vital_name}_confidence"

)

If a parser-specific confidence value is unavailable, the application searches the raw OCR results for a numerical match corresponding to the extracted vital.

For example, if the structured heart rate is 82, the algorithm examines OCR outputs for a numerical value matching 82 and retains the highest associated confidence.

For blood pressure, the function instead searches for OCR text containing a slash, reflecting the paired representation of the measurement.

The resulting confidence is classified into three presentation levels:

  • High: ≥ 0.80
  • Medium: 0.50–0.79
  • Low: < 0.50

These thresholds affect presentation only. They do not constitute experimentally validated probabilities of correct physiological extraction.

This distinction is important because OCR confidence is not necessarily equivalent to clinical correctness.

10. Data Validation and Defensive Programming

The interface includes several mechanisms intended to prevent malformed data from causing invalid displays or application failures.

The safe_int() function verifies that values are numerical and fall within specified limits before converting them to integers.

For example:

safe_int(

hr,

0,

300

)

is used to initialize the manually editable HR field.

The interface similarly imposes explicit numerical limits on user-entered verification values.

Examples include:

HR: 0–300 bpm

SpO₂: 0–100%

Systolic BP: 0–300 mmHg

Diastolic BP: 0–200 mmHg

RR: 0–100/min

EtCO₂: 0–150 mmHg

These bounds are primarily software safeguards rather than validated clinical reference ranges.

11. Human Verification Layer

A central feature of the architecture is the manual verification stage.

Extracted measurements are displayed to the user before being added to the longitudinal record.

The interface explicitly instructs the operator to compare the displayed values against the physical monitor.

The user can modify:

  • HR
  • SpO₂
  • systolic BP
  • diastolic BP
  • RR
  • EtCO₂

Only after the operator activates the verification control is the observation added to the historical dataset.

This produces a human-in-the-loop pipeline:

OCR extraction

↓

Automated parsing

↓

Displayed candidate values

↓

Human verification/correction

↓

Verified observation

This design substantially changes the interpretation of the resulting dataset. The longitudinal history represents user-confirmed values, rather than purely automated OCR output.

12. Temporal Data Representation

Verified observations are stored using Streamlit's session-state mechanism.

Each observation contains:

{

"time": datetime.now(),

"HR": verified_hr,

"SpO2": verified_spo2,

"BP Sys": verified_sys,

"BP Dia": verified_dia,

"RR": verified_rr,

"EtCO2": verified_etco2

}

Consequently, each record consists of a timestamp and six physiological variables.

The history is subsequently converted into a Pandas DataFrame:

df = pd.DataFrame(

st.session_state.history

)

This representation allows the observations to be displayed in tabular form and passed to downstream visualization and machine-learning routines.

13. Visualization of Physiological Trends

The temporal data are visualized using Plotly.

A line-and-marker trace is generated for:

  • HR
  • SpO₂
  • RR
  • EtCO₂

Blood pressure is retained in the tabular history but is not plotted in the provided trend graph.

Each variable is added as a separate Plotly trace:

go.Scatter(

x=chart_df["time"],

y=chart_df[column],

mode="lines+markers",

name=column

)

The visualization uses a white plotting template and includes labeled axes.

The purpose of the graph is descriptive: it allows an operator to inspect temporal trajectories rather than relying exclusively on individual measurements.

14. Machine-Learning Trend Analysis

A machine-learning subsystem is activated when at least three verified observations have been recorded.

The application dynamically imports:

from src.ml import (

train_trend_model,

predict_trend

)

The model is trained through:

model = train_trend_model()

and subsequently applied to the recorded history:

prediction, confidence, probabilities = (

predict_trend(

model,

st.session_state.history

)

)

The model returns three principal outputs:

  • A categorical trend prediction.
  • A model confidence value.
  • A dictionary of class probabilities.

The categorical output has three possible states:

Improving

Stable

Worsening

The interface presents the class probabilities separately.

Importantly, the provided code does not reveal the internal implementation of train_trend_model() or predict_trend(). Therefore, characteristics such as the machine-learning algorithm, feature engineering procedure, training-set size, class balance, validation strategy, and performance metrics cannot be scientifically established from the supplied interface code alone.

The application's own labeling appropriately identifies this component as a prototype trend estimator rather than a validated clinical deterioration score.

15. Clinical Reference Layer

The application contains a rule-based reference subsystem that evaluates selected physiological measurements against predefined thresholds.

The implementation evaluates:

  • HR > 100 bpm
  • HR < 60 bpm
  • SpO₂ < 94%
  • systolic BP < 90 mmHg
  • RR > 20/min
  • EtCO₂ < 35 mmHg

When a threshold is met, the corresponding pattern is displayed along with a list of possible clinical considerations.

For example, an elevated HR triggers a "tachycardia pattern" containing possible considerations such as physiological stress, fever, hypovolemia, hypoxemia, medication effects, and cardiac rhythm disturbance.

These rules are implemented using straightforward conditional statements rather than a probabilistic diagnostic model.

For example:

if (

isinstance(hr_value, (int, float))

and hr_value > 100

):

The output is therefore better characterized as a rule-based clinical reference layer rather than an automated diagnostic system.

The application explicitly communicates that these considerations are not diagnoses.

16. User Interface Design

The interface was implemented entirely within Streamlit.

The major interface sections are:

  • Patient context
  • Monitor image upload
  • Extracted vital signs
  • Verification controls
  • OCR details
  • Patient timeline
  • Trend graph
  • Machine-learning trend estimate
  • Clinical reference considerations

Custom CSS is embedded through Streamlit's Markdown functionality.

The styling creates:

  • high-contrast vital-sign cards,
  • confidence indicators,
  • warning panels,
  • reference panels,
  • a wide application layout,
  • visual separation between functional sections.

The design therefore emphasizes rapid interpretation of structured values while preserving access to the underlying OCR results.

17. Application State Management

Because Streamlit applications rerun portions of the Python script when users interact with widgets, persistent information is maintained through st.session_state.

Three principal state variables are initialized:

st.session_state.vitals

st.session_state.ocr

st.session_state.history

They represent:

State variablePurpose
vitalsMost recently parsed physiological values
ocrMost recent OCR output
historyUser-verified longitudinal observations

This state model allows the application to preserve the patient's recorded timeline across interface interactions during the active application session.

The supplied implementation does not show persistent database storage. Therefore, the history should be interpreted as session-level application state rather than a permanent medical record.

18. Error Handling

The principal image-processing workflow is enclosed in a try/except block.

If OCR, parsing, blood-pressure extraction, or another operation raises an exception, the interface reports the error rather than terminating the entire application.

Similarly, machine-learning execution is isolated within its own error-handling block:

try:

...

except Exception as e:

st.warning(

f"ML trend model unavailable: {e}"

)

This allows the core extraction and visualization workflow to remain usable if the optional trend-analysis subsystem fails.

19. Safety-Oriented Design

The prototype incorporates several safeguards intended to reduce inappropriate interpretation.

First, automated OCR values are explicitly presented as values requiring verification.

Second, the application separates extracted values from verified values.

Third, the machine-learning component is explicitly labeled as a prototype trend estimate.

Fourth, the clinical-reference layer is explicitly described as non-diagnostic.

Finally, the interface instructs users to compare extracted values with the original monitor and patient assessment.

These design decisions establish a decision-support boundary in which the software assists with transcription and visualization but does not replace clinical assessment.

20. Discussion

The implemented architecture demonstrates how multiple relatively simple computational components can be combined into an end-to-end physiological-data pipeline.

The first contribution is the integration of image-based extraction with structured physiological parsing. Rather than requiring manual transcription from every monitor photograph, OCR can provide candidate numerical values that are subsequently normalized into a predefined schema.

The second contribution is the use of a specialized blood-pressure extraction pathway. Blood pressure presents a different parsing problem because its two components must be identified together. Regular-expression matching and physiological plausibility filtering provide a lightweight mechanism for rejecting obviously inappropriate candidates.

The third contribution is the human-verification architecture. Instead of assuming OCR output is correct, the system explicitly inserts a human confirmation stage before measurements enter the longitudinal dataset. This is particularly important because OCR errors may result from glare, blur, image perspective, character segmentation, monitor typography, or overlapping graphical elements.

The fourth contribution is the integration of temporal visualization. Once measurements are verified, individual observations can be transformed into a time series, making changes in HR, SpO₂, RR, and EtCO₂ easier to inspect.

Finally, the prototype demonstrates how a machine-learning layer can be incorporated after data acquisition. However, the usefulness of such a model depends strongly on the quality, size, representativeness, labeling methodology, and validation of its training data.

21. Limitations

Several limitations should be considered.

21.1 OCR Performance

OCR accuracy is dependent on the quality of the input image and the underlying OCR implementation. The provided code does not specify the OCR engine, preprocessing operations, image segmentation strategy, character-recognition architecture, or benchmark performance.

Consequently, sensitivity and specificity for individual vital signs cannot be calculated from the interface code alone.

21.2 Monitor Variability

Different monitor manufacturers and models may use different fonts, layouts, colors, abbreviations, and numerical arrangements. A parser developed around one display configuration may therefore perform differently on another.

21.3 Blood-Pressure Parsing

The blood-pressure regular expression assumes a relatively conventional numerical representation. Alternative display formats may not be recognized.

The numerical plausibility constraints also prevent certain values from being selected even if they were correctly displayed by an unusual monitor configuration.

21.4 Confidence Interpretation

OCR confidence is used as a proxy for extraction reliability, but it should not automatically be interpreted as the probability that the physiological value is clinically correct.

21.5 Machine-Learning Validation

The machine-learning implementation is external to the supplied interface code. The training data, feature construction, model architecture, class definitions, cross-validation strategy, and independent test performance are not provided.

Therefore, no claims regarding model accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, calibration, generalizability, or clinical utility can be made from the supplied code.

21.6 Limited Temporal Data

The machine-learning component requires only three observations before producing an estimate. From a scientific perspective, three observations may provide very limited information about a physiological trajectory.

The minimum-observation requirement should therefore not be confused with evidence that three measurements are sufficient for reliable clinical trend prediction.

21.7 Lack of Persistent Clinical Storage

The supplied application stores historical measurements in Streamlit session state. No electronic health record integration, database layer, audit log, or durable patient-record mechanism is demonstrated.

21.8 Rule-Based Reference Thresholds

The clinical reference subsystem uses fixed numerical thresholds. Physiological interpretation can depend on age, baseline physiology, clinical context, treatment, environment, and measurement conditions. Consequently, threshold-triggered text should not be interpreted as individualized diagnosis.

22. Reproducibility and Future Evaluation

A rigorous evaluation of the prototype would require a dedicated dataset of monitor photographs with ground-truth annotations.

A suitable evaluation protocol could contain the following stages:

Stage 1: Image Dataset Construction

Collect monitor images representing different:

  • monitor manufacturers,
  • display layouts,
  • lighting conditions,
  • camera angles,
  • image resolutions,
  • patient-monitor configurations,
  • physiological value ranges.
Stage 2: Ground-Truth Annotation

Each image should be manually annotated for:

  • HR,
  • SpO₂,
  • systolic BP,
  • diastolic BP,
  • RR,
  • EtCO₂.

The ground truth should be independently verified against the original monitor output.

Stage 3: OCR Evaluation

Measure:

  • character-level recognition accuracy,
  • numerical recognition accuracy,
  • vital-sign extraction accuracy,
  • false-positive rate,
  • missing-value rate.
Stage 4: Parser Evaluation

Compare parsed values with ground truth and calculate variable-specific metrics.

Stage 5: Blood-Pressure Evaluation

Evaluate systolic and diastolic pressure independently and jointly, including cases containing visually ambiguous characters.

Stage 6: Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation

Measure the proportion of OCR outputs requiring manual correction and the time required to verify each observation.

Stage 7: Machine-Learning Evaluation

For the trend model, an independent dataset should be used for testing.

Potential metrics include:

  • accuracy,
  • precision,
  • recall,
  • F1 score,
  • confusion matrix,
  • calibration,
  • class-specific sensitivity,
  • temporal generalization.

Importantly, the test data should remain independent from the training data to prevent optimistic performance estimates.

23. Proposed Experimental Methodology

A formal study could compare three workflows:

Workflow A — Manual transcription

Monitor image → Human reads → Manual entry

Workflow B — OCR-assisted transcription

Monitor image → OCR → Human verification

Workflow C — Automated extraction

Monitor image → OCR → Parser → Automated record

Workflow B would be particularly informative because it reflects the architecture implemented in the prototype.

Primary outcome measures could include:

  • Time required to produce a verified vital-sign record.
  • Numerical transcription error rate.
  • Percentage of observations requiring correction.
  • Agreement between extracted and ground-truth values.
  • User-reported workload.

This experimental design would permit assessment of whether OCR assistance reduces transcription burden while maintaining human oversight.

24. Ethical and Clinical Considerations

A system processing physiological information must distinguish between technical extraction and clinical interpretation.

The prototype's architecture appropriately separates these functions. OCR identifies candidate information from an image; verification establishes the values that enter the historical record; visualization represents temporal data; and the reference layer provides possible contextual considerations.

None of these operations independently establishes a diagnosis.

Before deployment in clinical environments, additional considerations would include:

  • patient privacy,
  • secure image handling,
  • access control,
  • auditability,
  • data retention,
  • model validation,
  • clinical governance,
  • usability testing,
  • regulatory classification,
  • human-factors evaluation,
  • monitoring for systematic extraction errors.

In particular, performance should be evaluated across the diversity of monitor displays and clinical contexts in which the system is intended to operate.

25. Conclusion

This paper describes an educational prototype that combines computer vision, OCR, rule-based numerical parsing, human verification, temporal data visualization, machine-learning trend estimation, and clinical reference rules within a single Python-based application.

The architecture follows a sequential human-in-the-loop workflow:

Image

↓

OCR

↓

Structured parsing

↓

Confidence assessment

↓

Human verification

↓

Timestamped physiological history

↓

Visualization

↓

Prototype trend analysis

↓

Reference considerations

The principal engineering feature is the separation between automated extraction and verified clinical data. This approach recognizes that OCR output can contain errors and therefore should not automatically become part of a longitudinal physiological record.

The prototype demonstrates the technical feasibility of transforming photographs of physiological monitors into structured observations and subsequently analyzing those observations over time. Nevertheless, the current implementation does not provide evidence of clinical accuracy or clinical effectiveness. In particular, the OCR subsystem, parsing subsystem, and machine-learning model require independent validation before quantitative claims regarding performance can be established.

Accordingly, the system is best understood as a research and educational prototype illustrating the integration of computer vision and machine learning into physiological-data workflows rather than as an autonomous diagnostic or clinical decision-making system.

AI EMS Assessment Prototype Prototype development notes
1. Project Title

Development of an Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning EMS Injury Assessment Prototype Combining Computer Vision, Machine Learning, and Protocol-Based Information

2. Project Overview

The AI EMS Assessment system was developed as an experimental software prototype designed to demonstrate how artificial intelligence could combine image classification and patient information within a single EMS-oriented interface.

The system combines three primary components:

  • Computer vision for classification of injury photographs.
  • Machine learning for a prototype risk estimate based on patient information and vital signs.
  • Protocol-based information associated with the predicted injury category.

The system was implemented using Python and Streamlit. The computer-vision component uses a ResNet-18 neural network architecture through the timm library. The risk component uses a previously trained machine-learning model loaded through joblib.

The prototype was developed for educational and research purposes and was not designed or validated as an autonomous clinical decision-making system.

3. Development Objective

The primary development objective was to create a functional prototype capable of accepting two forms of information:

Patient information
  • Age
  • Pain score
  • Heart rate
  • Systolic blood pressure
  • Diastolic blood pressure
  • SpO₂
  • Respiratory rate
  • GCS
Visual information
  • Injury photograph

The system processes these inputs and produces an integrated output containing:

  • Predicted injury classification
  • Model confidence
  • Classification probabilities
  • Patient vital signs
  • Prototype risk estimate
  • Screening flags
  • Protocol-based considerations
  • Model limitations

Streamlit was selected to provide a simple interface between the user and the underlying machine-learning models.

7. Patient Input Module

The patient-input module was developed using Streamlit input controls.

The user can enter:

Age

Pain

Heart Rate

Systolic Blood Pressure

Diastolic Blood Pressure

SpO₂

Respiratory Rate

GCS

Each variable has an appropriate numerical range within the interface.

For example, heart rate is restricted to a range of 0–300, while GCS is restricted to 3–15.

The values are collected and organized into a pandas DataFrame.

The resulting structure is:

age

heart_rate

systolic_bp

diastolic_bp

spo2

respiratory_rate

gcs

This structure is passed to the trained risk model.

8. Injury Image Module

The image-analysis component allows the user to upload an injury photograph.

The application accepts:

.jpg

.jpeg

When an image is uploaded, it is opened using Pillow and converted to RGB format.

This standardizes the image representation before it is passed to the neural network.

9. Image Preprocessing

Before being analyzed by the neural network, each image passes through a preprocessing pipeline.

The image is resized to:

224 × 224 pixels

It is then converted to a PyTorch tensor.

Finally, the tensor is normalized using:

Mean:

[0.485, 0.456, 0.406]

Standard deviation:

[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]

The resulting tensor is expanded to include a batch dimension before being passed to the neural network.

The preprocessing pipeline can be represented as:

Original Image

↓

RGB Conversion

↓

224 × 224 Resize

↓

Tensor Conversion

↓

Normalization

↓

Batch Dimension

↓

Neural Network

10. Computer-Vision Model

The computer-vision component uses a ResNet-18 convolutional neural network architecture.

The model is created using the timm library.

The application does not use pretrained ImageNet weights during inference. Instead, it creates a ResNet-18 architecture with the number of output classes determined by the classes stored in the trained checkpoint.

The trained model parameters are loaded from:

injury_model.pth

The checkpoint contains:

model_state

classes

The model_state contains the learned neural-network parameters.

The classes value provides the injury categories recognized by the model.

11. Model Loading

The trained model is loaded using PyTorch.

The checkpoint is loaded with:

map_location="cpu"

This allows the prototype to run inference on a computer without requiring a dedicated GPU.

After loading the trained parameters, the model is placed into evaluation mode.

This ensures that the model operates as an inference model rather than performing training operations.

12. Prediction Process

When the user selects:

RUN AI ASSESSMENT

the uploaded image is transformed into the required tensor representation.

The tensor is then passed through the injury-classification model.

The neural network produces a vector of output values corresponding to the possible injury classes.

These raw outputs are converted into probabilities using the softmax function.

Conceptually:

Model Output

↓

Softmax

↓

Class Probabilities

↓

Highest Probability

↓

Predicted Injury

The class with the highest probability is selected as the model's predicted injury.

13. Confidence Calculation

The highest probability produced by the softmax function is displayed as the model's confidence.

For example:

Abrasion 0.82

Burn 0.07

Cut 0.08

Laceration 0.03

The system would report:

Predicted Finding: Abrasion

Confidence: 82%

The application also displays the complete probability distribution as a bar chart.

This allows the user to see not only the selected prediction but also the model's relative probabilities for other classes.

14. Risk-Model Development and Integration

A separate machine-learning model is loaded from:

risk_model.pkl

The model is loaded using joblib.

The application constructs a single patient-data row containing:

age

heart_rate

systolic_bp

diastolic_bp

spo2

respiratory_rate

gcs

pain

The data are passed to the model for prediction.

The model generates:

  • A predicted risk class.
  • Probabilities for the available risk classes.

The application obtains these values through the model's:

predict()

predict_proba()

methods.

15. Risk-Output Display

The prototype displays the predicted risk category using three visual states:

High → Red

Moderate → Yellow

Low → Green

The probabilities for each available risk class are also displayed.

For example:

High: 15%

Moderate: 25%

Low: 60%

These values represent the output of the trained prototype model.

Because the risk model was trained using synthetic data, the output is explicitly described in the application as a prototype risk estimate rather than a validated clinical risk assessment.

16. Rule-Based Screening Layer

In addition to the machine-learning models, the system contains a simple rule-based screening layer.

The prototype checks several patient variables.

The implemented conditions include:

Heart rate > 120

Systolic BP < 90

SpO₂ < 92

Respiratory rate > 28

GCS < 13

Pain ≥ 8

When a threshold is exceeded or falls below the specified value, the system adds a corresponding screening finding.

For example:

Heart rate > 120

↓

Prototype screening flag

This component is intentionally transparent: unlike the neural network, the conditions are explicitly defined in the software.

17. Findings Module

The findings module combines the image-classification result with the rule-based screening information.

The first finding reports the image classifier's prediction and confidence.

Additional findings are generated if the patient's input values meet any of the prototype screening thresholds.

If no additional thresholds are triggered, the application reports that no additional prototype screening flags were triggered.

This creates a simple summary of the information processed by the application.

18. Protocol Module

The application includes a separate protocol-information component:

protocols.py

The predicted injury class is passed to:

get_protocol(predicted_class)

The function returns protocol-related information including:

title

considerations

The application displays the title and individual considerations.

The application also displays:

PROTOCOL_SOURCE

PROTOCOL_NOTE

This design separates protocol information from the machine-learning model itself.

Therefore, protocol content can be updated independently from the neural-network model.

19. Caching and Performance

The application uses Streamlit's resource caching mechanism:

@st.cache_resource

This is applied to the model-loading functions.

The purpose is to prevent the trained models from being repeatedly loaded every time Streamlit reruns the application.

This improves application responsiveness and reduces unnecessary model-loading operations.

20. Safety and Limitations by Design

Several limitations are explicitly incorporated into the software.

The application states that:

  • The system is an educational/research prototype.
  • The computer-vision model was trained on a limited wound-image dataset.
  • Validation accuracy does not constitute clinical validation.
  • The risk model was trained using synthetic data.
  • Model confidence does not represent clinical certainty.
  • Protocol considerations must be checked against current local guidance.

These statements are included to distinguish software/model performance from clinical validation.

21. Development Testing

After development, the system was evaluated using a test set of 100 injury images.

The evaluation compared the AI's predicted injury classification with the reference classification.

The results were:

MeasurementResult
Images tested100
Correct classifications94
Incorrect classifications6
Overall accuracy94%
Highest-confidence prediction correct90%

The model therefore achieved an observed classification accuracy of:

94%

on the evaluated 100-image dataset.

22. Interpretation of Development Results

The 94% result demonstrates the performance of the implemented model on the particular test dataset used in the evaluation.

It does not demonstrate that the system will achieve 94% accuracy on all injury photographs.

The difference between the 94% classification accuracy and the 90% highest-confidence correctness rate also indicates that the model's confidence output should not be treated as equivalent to diagnostic certainty.

The six incorrectly classified images should be retained for error analysis rather than removed from the evaluation.

25. Scientific Development Summary

The AI EMS Assessment prototype was developed as a modular Python-based system combining computer vision, machine learning, rule-based screening, and protocol information.

A ResNet-18 convolutional neural network was used for injury-image classification. Uploaded images were converted to RGB format, resized to 224 × 224 pixels, converted to tensors, normalized, and processed by the trained network. Softmax probabilities were used to identify the highest-probability injury classification.

A separate machine-learning model processed patient characteristics and vital signs to generate a prototype risk estimate. A rule-based layer independently identified predefined screening thresholds. Finally, a protocol module associated the predicted injury category with informational protocol considerations.

The integrated system was implemented using Streamlit to provide an interactive interface for entering patient information, uploading images, and viewing model outputs.

In an initial evaluation using 100 injury images, the injury classifier correctly identified 94 images (94%). The highest-confidence prediction corresponded to the reference classification in 90 cases (90%).

These results provide an initial technical evaluation of the prototype. They do not establish clinical validity, clinical safety, or effectiveness. Further testing with larger, independent, and appropriately representative datasets would be required before drawing conclusions about real-world clinical performance.

Development of Paramedic AI Scientist: An Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Platform for EMS Evidence Review, Hypothesis Generation, and Computational Research Research paper / viewpoint

Development of Paramedic AI Scientist: An Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Platform for EMS Evidence Review, Hypothesis Generation, and Computational Research

Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly being investigated as tools for scientific literature analysis, hypothesis generation, data analysis, and computational experimentation. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential for generating scientific hypotheses and assisting researchers with complex knowledge-based tasks, although their outputs require independent validation and expert oversight. Recent research has specifically investigated the use of LLMs for automated scientific hypothesis generation and has demonstrated both the potential and limitations of this approach [1,2].

This paper describes the development of Paramedic AI Scientist, a Python-based artificial intelligence research assistant designed for emergency medical services (EMS) evidence review, clinical research, patient simulation, clinical prediction, retrospective data analysis, and quality-improvement research. The system integrates scientific literature retrieval, AI-generated hypothesis development, experiment selection, Python code generation, controlled computational execution, result analysis, experiment storage, and automated research-report generation within a Streamlit-based web application.

The system additionally incorporates structured EMS patient-case representation using PatientCase and VitalSigns models, allowing users to enter demographic information, chief complaint, relevant history, physical examination findings, and physiological observations including heart rate, respiratory rate, SpO₂, and ETCO₂.

A distinguishing feature of Paramedic AI Scientist is its ability to generate computational experiments from natural-language research questions. Generated Python code is cleaned, inspected for prohibited operations, executed within a temporary file with a 60-second execution limit, and subsequently analyzed by the AI system. Experimental code, outputs, and analyses are retained as structured research history and can be incorporated into an automatically generated final research report.

The application is intended as a research and educational prototype rather than an autonomous clinical decision-making system. AI-generated hypotheses, software, interpretations, and conclusions require human verification. The paper describes the system architecture, research workflow, code-execution safeguards, EMS case integration, limitations, and potential future applications.

Keywords

artificial intelligence; large language models; emergency medical services; paramedic education; scientific research; hypothesis generation; computational experiments; clinical research; EMS research; Python; Streamlit; machine learning

Introduction

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being investigated as an instrument for supporting scientific research. Large language models can process large quantities of textual information, generate candidate hypotheses, summarize evidence, write computational code, and assist with analytical workflows. Recent research has specifically explored the use of LLMs for scientific hypothesis generation, including systems designed to generate hypotheses from open-domain scientific information [1,2].

Zhou et al. investigated hypothesis generation using LLMs and reported that generated hypotheses could improve predictive performance in several experimental settings while also identifying insights that were consistent with established theories or potentially novel for the evaluated tasks [1]. Yang et al. subsequently investigated automated open-domain scientific hypothesis discovery using LLMs and described a multi-module approach for generating and evaluating scientific hypotheses from broad textual information [2].

The potential role of LLMs in scientific research has also progressed beyond purely textual hypothesis generation. Recent experimental research has investigated LLM-generated scientific hypotheses followed by laboratory testing, demonstrating a workflow in which AI-generated propositions can be subjected to empirical evaluation rather than being accepted solely on the basis of language-model output [3].

These developments suggest a possible model in which AI assists with several stages of the research process while empirical experimentation remains responsible for determining whether a proposed hypothesis is supported.

Paramedic AI Scientist was developed as a prototype based on this concept, adapted specifically for EMS and paramedic-oriented research.

Rather than functioning solely as a conversational chatbot, the system provides a structured research workflow:

Research Question → Literature Search → Hypothesis Generation → Experiment Selection → Python Experiment Generation → Code Validation → Experiment Execution → Result Analysis → Research History → Final Research Report

The application is designed to demonstrate how these functions can be integrated into a single research environment.

System Overview

Paramedic AI Scientist is implemented as a Python-based web application using Streamlit.

The application provides a graphical interface through which the user can define a research question, select a research mode, configure the number of experiments, construct an EMS patient case, initiate literature retrieval, review generated hypotheses, execute computational experiments, inspect experimental results, and generate a final research report.

The system provides six research modes:

  • Clinical Evidence Review
  • EMS Protocol Research
  • Clinical Prediction Model
  • Patient Simulation
  • Retrospective Data Analysis
  • Quality Improvement

The research mode provides contextual organization for the intended research activity, while the natural-language research question serves as the principal input to the scientific workflow.

The application also provides an experiment-count control allowing between one and five experiments to be requested within a research session. The interface recommends one to three experiments under current API constraints.

Natural-Language Research Questions

The research workflow begins with a natural-language research question.

Users are not required to specify a programming language, statistical test, dataset structure, or experimental procedure manually. Instead, the question is provided to the AI research system, which subsequently determines potential hypotheses and experimental approaches.

This design attempts to lower the technical barrier to computational research by allowing a researcher or student to begin with a conventional scientific question.

For example, a question could investigate whether one machine-learning algorithm performs better than another on a defined dataset, whether a particular predictive feature improves classification, or whether a simulated EMS intervention produces a measurable difference under specified conditions.

The system does not assume that the generated experiment constitutes valid scientific evidence. Rather, the natural-language question serves as the starting point from which candidate research approaches are developed.

Scientific Literature Search

The first research stage is literature retrieval.

When the user initiates a research session, the application calls the search_papers() function using the research question as the search input.

The current implementation requests a maximum of three papers.

Retrieved papers are stored in Streamlit session state and presented within expandable interface components. For each paper, the application displays the available title, abstract, and author information.

This stage provides an external evidence component before hypothesis generation.

The separation is important because the application does not rely exclusively on the language model's internal knowledge. Instead, retrieved scientific literature is explicitly supplied to the hypothesis-generation function.

This general architecture is consistent with broader research into retrieval-supported language-model systems, where external information retrieval can supplement knowledge encoded within a language model [4].

The current implementation searches arXiv, meaning that the retrieved material should not automatically be interpreted as equivalent to peer-reviewed clinical literature. A future implementation could incorporate additional bibliographic databases and distinguish peer-reviewed publications, preprints, guidelines, systematic reviews, and other source types.

AI-Assisted Hypothesis Generation

After literature retrieval, Paramedic AI Scientist calls generate_hypotheses().

The function receives both the original research question and the retrieved papers.

The system is designed to produce structured hypotheses rather than a single conversational answer.

Each hypothesis can contain:

  • Hypothesis
  • Reasoning
  • Proposed experiment
  • Expected result
  • Falsification criteria

The inclusion of a falsification field is particularly relevant to scientific reasoning because the system is encouraged to identify conditions under which the proposed hypothesis would not be supported.

The design therefore attempts to distinguish between:

  • "What might be true?"
  • "What experiment could demonstrate that it is not true?"

This structure reflects emerging research into LLM-supported scientific hypothesis generation. However, the existence of an AI-generated hypothesis does not establish novelty, plausibility, causality, or scientific validity. Independent review and empirical testing remain necessary [1–3].

Hypothesis Selection and Experiment Planning

Following hypothesis generation, the application invokes choose_experiment().

The function receives three principal inputs:

  1. The original research question.
  2. The generated hypotheses.
  3. The history of experiments already conducted during the current session.

The returned decision identifies a selected hypothesis and an experiment goal.

The selected hypothesis and experiment goal are explicitly displayed within the interface.

This design creates an intermediate planning stage between hypothesis generation and code generation.

The architecture therefore does not immediately convert the first generated hypothesis into executable code. Instead, an experiment-selection component is used to determine which proposed investigation should be pursued.

The inclusion of previous experiment history also creates the possibility of iterative research. Subsequent experiments can be selected with knowledge of earlier computational results.

AI-Generated Computational Experiments

After an experiment has been selected, the system invokes generate_experiment().

The function receives:

  • The research question.
  • The selected hypothesis.
  • The experiment goal.

It then generates Python source code intended to test the proposed research question.

The application immediately passes the generated code through clean_python_code().

The generated Python code is subsequently displayed to the user in an expandable code section.

This is an important transparency feature because the user can inspect the computational methodology generated by the AI rather than seeing only the final result.

The architecture consequently separates three distinct elements:

  • AI-generated methodology
  • Executable computational procedure
  • Experimental result

This distinction is important because a computational result is only meaningful in relation to the code and assumptions that produced it.

AI-Generated Code and Scientific Reproducibility

The system retains the generated Python code as part of each experiment record.

Each experimental record includes:

  • Experiment number
  • Selected hypothesis
  • Experiment goal
  • Generated Python code
  • Experimental output
  • Scientific analysis

This allows the computational procedure to be retained alongside its result.

Such preservation is important for reproducibility because a research conclusion cannot be meaningfully reproduced if the computational procedure that produced it is unavailable.

Future versions could extend this functionality by storing additional metadata including Python version, package versions, dataset identifiers, random seeds, model identifiers, timestamps, and execution-environment information.

These additions would make it possible to distinguish between merely recording an AI-generated answer and creating a reproducible computational research artifact.

Generated-Code Safety Controls

A particularly significant feature of Paramedic AI Scientist is that it executes AI-generated Python code.

Because generated code can potentially contain unsafe operations, the application includes an explicit validation layer before execution.

The validate_experiment_code() function compares the generated source against a list of prohibited patterns.

The current implementation blocks operations associated with:

  • os.system
  • subprocess
  • shutil
  • socket
  • requests
  • urllib
  • httpx
  • exec()
  • eval()
  • __import__
  • import os
  • import sys
  • import subprocess

If a prohibited pattern is identified, the experiment is blocked and the system reports the potentially unsafe operation.

The need for such controls is supported by emerging research on LLM-generated code security. Recent research has demonstrated that AI-generated source code can contain security vulnerabilities and that code-generation security remains an active area of investigation [5,6].

The validation system used by Paramedic AI Scientist should therefore be regarded as a basic application-level safeguard rather than a complete security sandbox.

Pattern matching cannot guarantee that arbitrary generated code is safe.

A production implementation would require stronger isolation, potentially including:

  • Containerized execution
  • Restricted filesystem access
  • Network isolation
  • Resource quotas
  • Non-privileged execution
  • Process isolation
  • Dependency restrictions
  • System-call restrictions
  • Runtime monitoring
  • Independent security testing

This distinction is particularly important because the current application uses Python's subprocess.run() to execute the generated experiment after the source-level validation stage.

Controlled Experiment Execution

Validated experiment code is written to a temporary Python file using tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile().

The generated program is then executed using a separate Python process.

The execution environment sets:

PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8

This is intended to provide consistent handling of Unicode output, particularly on Windows systems.

The experiment captures standard output and standard error.

Successful standard output is returned as the experiment result.

If the experiment generates warnings through standard error, those warnings are appended to the displayed output.

If the experiment terminates with an error, the application reports the error and includes the relevant portion of the generated error output.

A 60-second execution timeout is also implemented.

If the experiment exceeds the time limit, execution is terminated and the system reports that the experiment exceeded the permitted runtime.

Temporary experiment files are subsequently removed.

The result is therefore a controlled computational workflow rather than unrestricted execution from the user interface.

Experimental Result Analysis

After execution, the experimental output is passed to analyze_results().

The analysis function receives:

  • Research question
  • Selected hypothesis
  • Experimental output

The AI-generated analysis is then presented in a dedicated Scientific Analysis section.

This architecture separates the computational experiment from its natural-language interpretation.

The Python program produces the computational result.

The AI analysis component subsequently interprets that result in relation to the research question and hypothesis.

This distinction is important because the AI-generated analysis is not itself the experiment. It is an interpretation of the experiment's output.

A future implementation could improve this process by incorporating formal statistical validation, confidence intervals, effect sizes, hypothesis tests, model-performance metrics, assumption checking, and automated detection of common statistical errors before an AI-generated interpretation is presented.

Research History

Paramedic AI Scientist maintains research history using Streamlit session state.

Three primary session-state objects are initialized:

  • history
  • papers
  • hypotheses

The research history contains structured records for completed experiments.

Each record contains the experiment number, hypothesis, goal, generated code, output, and analysis.

This enables the application to display previous experiments during the current session and to supply earlier experimental results to subsequent experiment-selection operations.

The history therefore acts as a lightweight research-memory mechanism within the application.

Experiment Persistence

In addition to temporary Streamlit session history, the application invokes save_experiment() after each completed experiment.

The saved record includes the original research question, experiment number, hypothesis, generated code, output, and analysis.

This provides a mechanism for preserving individual experiments beyond the immediate display of results.

Persistent experiment storage is potentially important for research auditability because it allows the researcher to examine not only what the system concluded but also what computational procedure was generated and executed.

Iterative Research

The application supports multiple experiments within a single research session.

The experiment loop repeats the following sequence:

  1. Select an experiment.
  2. Identify the selected hypothesis.
  3. Define an experiment goal.
  4. Generate Python code.
  5. Clean the generated code.
  6. Validate the code.
  7. Execute the experiment.
  8. Capture the result.
  9. Analyze the result.
  10. Record the experiment.
  11. Save the experiment.

The experiment history is then available to subsequent iterations.

This provides the architecture for an iterative research process rather than a single-question/single-answer interaction.

The approach is conceptually related to emerging research into AI systems that connect hypothesis generation with experimental evaluation. Importantly, however, Paramedic AI Scientist performs computational experiments within a software environment and should not be represented as a fully autonomous scientific laboratory system [3].

EMS Patient Case Integration

Paramedic AI Scientist incorporates structured EMS patient information through two imported models:

  • PatientCase
  • VitalSigns

The interface allows the user to enter:

  • Age
  • Sex
  • Chief complaint
  • Relevant medical history
  • Physical examination findings
  • Heart rate
  • Respiratory rate
  • SpO₂
  • ETCO₂

Relevant history is converted from comma-separated text into a structured list.

Vital signs are represented using the VitalSigns model.

The complete case is then represented as a PatientCase object.

This provides a structured representation of an EMS encounter that can potentially be used by future research modules.

The current code constructs the patient object independently of the experiment-generation workflow. This means that, in the implementation provided, the patient case is available within the application but is not automatically supplied to the literature-search, hypothesis-generation, experiment-generation, or analysis functions.

This distinction is technically important.

The current architecture therefore provides patient-case infrastructure, while future development could explicitly connect the patient-case object to research experiments and simulations.

EMS Research Modes

The application provides six research modes.

Clinical Evidence Review

This mode provides a framework for examining evidence related to clinical questions.

Potential future functionality could include structured evidence grading, systematic literature comparison, and citation extraction.

EMS Protocol Research

This mode is intended for questions involving EMS protocols and clinical practice.

Because EMS protocols vary by jurisdiction and agency, any future implementation should distinguish general evidence from locally applicable protocol requirements.

Clinical Prediction Model

This mode provides a conceptual environment for investigating predictive models using structured clinical variables.

The current application does not itself implement a validated clinical prediction model merely because this mode exists. It provides a research context within which an AI-generated computational experiment could potentially investigate predictive modeling.

Patient Simulation

The patient-case structure provides a foundation for simulated EMS research scenarios.

The current implementation captures demographic, complaint, history, examination, and selected physiological variables.

Future versions could use this structured representation to create longitudinal or dynamic patient simulations.

Retrospective Data Analysis

This mode provides a conceptual framework for analyzing existing datasets.

Any implementation using real patient information would require appropriate privacy, security, governance, de-identification, and research-ethics controls.

Quality Improvement

The quality-improvement mode provides a framework for research questions concerning EMS processes and performance.

Future versions could incorporate structured quality metrics, statistical process-control methods, and de-identified operational datasets.

Final Research Report

Once at least one experiment has been completed, the application invokes generate_final_report().

The final report receives:

  • The research question.
  • Retrieved scientific papers.
  • Generated hypotheses.
  • Complete experimental history.

The resulting report is displayed within the Streamlit interface.

The application also provides a download button allowing the report to be downloaded as a Markdown document named:

research_report.md

The final-report component therefore consolidates the research process into a single document.

Importantly, the final report is itself AI-generated. It should therefore be considered a draft research artifact requiring human review rather than an independently verified scientific publication.

Software Architecture

The principal architecture of Paramedic AI Scientist consists of several interconnected layers.

EMS Model Layer

Provides structured representations of patient cases and vital signs through PatientCase and VitalSigns.

Safety Layer

Provides the research_disclaimer() function used to communicate the research and educational nature of the system.

Literature Layer

Uses search_papers() to retrieve relevant scientific papers.

Hypothesis Layer

Uses generate_hypotheses() to generate structured candidate hypotheses.

Experiment-Selection Layer

Uses choose_experiment() to identify the hypothesis and experimental objective to investigate.

Code-Generation Layer

Uses generate_experiment() to produce Python experimental code.

Code-Processing Layer

Uses clean_python_code() to process generated source code before validation and execution.

Security Layer

Uses validate_experiment_code() to block predefined potentially unsafe operations.

Execution Layer

Uses a temporary Python file and subprocess.run() to execute validated experiments under a 60-second timeout.

Analysis Layer

Uses analyze_results() to interpret computational output.

Persistence Layer

Uses save_experiment() and Streamlit session state to retain experimental information.

Reporting Layer

Uses generate_final_report() to consolidate research information into a downloadable report.

Interface Layer

Streamlit provides the graphical user interface and coordinates the complete research workflow.

Research Transparency

A central design principle of Paramedic AI Scientist is that the intermediate stages of the research process are visible to the user.

The interface displays:

  • Retrieved literature
  • Generated hypotheses
  • Hypothesis reasoning
  • Proposed experiments
  • Expected results
  • Falsification criteria
  • Selected hypothesis
  • Experiment goal
  • Generated Python code
  • Experimental output
  • Scientific analysis
  • Final research report

This is preferable to an architecture in which the system provides only a final AI-generated conclusion.

Displaying intermediate artifacts allows the researcher to inspect the assumptions and computational procedures underlying the result.

However, visibility does not guarantee correctness. An AI-generated hypothesis or code sample may appear scientifically plausible while still containing conceptual, statistical, or programming errors.

Safety and Human Oversight

Paramedic AI Scientist operates in an EMS and healthcare research context, making human oversight particularly important.

The system is explicitly designed as a research assistant and includes a research disclaimer.

AI-generated hypotheses should not automatically be interpreted as scientifically valid.

AI-generated Python code should not automatically be assumed to be correct.

Computational results should not automatically be interpreted as clinically meaningful.

AI-generated analyses should not automatically be treated as expert statistical interpretation.

Final reports should not automatically be treated as publication-ready scientific manuscripts.

These limitations are consistent with emerging research showing both the potential and uncertainty of LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation [1–3].

The distinction between research assistance and clinical decision support is especially important. A computational experiment performed by the system does not constitute clinical validation, and an AI-generated conclusion should not be used as a substitute for professional clinical judgment.

Security Considerations

The ability to generate and execute Python code creates a unique security requirement.

The current implementation attempts to reduce risk through source-code pattern blocking and execution time limits.

However, the implementation should not be characterized as a secure sandbox.

The blocked-pattern approach is inherently limited because unsafe behavior can potentially be expressed in ways that do not match the predefined strings.

Furthermore, executing generated Python through subprocess.run() means that the Python interpreter ultimately has access to the permissions of the host environment.

Research into LLM-generated code has identified security vulnerabilities as an important concern, supporting the need for stronger isolation when AI-generated software is executed automatically [5,6].

A production-grade version should therefore move code execution into a dedicated sandbox with restricted privileges and no unnecessary access to the host operating system or network.

Scientific Validity and Limitations

Several limitations apply to the current implementation.

First, the application does not itself establish the scientific validity of generated hypotheses.

Second, the literature search currently retrieves a maximum of three papers. This is appropriate for a prototype but is insufficient for a systematic literature review.

Third, the current implementation searches arXiv rather than providing comprehensive coverage of biomedical and EMS bibliographic databases. Retrieved papers may therefore include preprints and should be independently assessed for peer-review status and methodological quality.

Fourth, the hypothesis-generation component is dependent on the capabilities and limitations of the underlying language model.

Fifth, AI-generated Python code may contain methodological or programming errors.

Sixth, the current code-validation approach is not a complete security boundary.

Seventh, the application does not currently demonstrate formal statistical validation of AI-generated experimental methodology.

Eighth, the structured EMS patient case is currently created within the interface but is not directly passed into the research functions shown in the provided implementation.

Ninth, no formal evaluation has yet established that Paramedic AI Scientist improves EMS research productivity, scientific reasoning, research quality, or educational outcomes.

Finally, the system should not be interpreted as a validated clinical decision-support system.

Future Development

Future development could address several areas.

Expanded Literature Retrieval

The literature component could be expanded beyond a three-paper arXiv search to include biomedical and scientific databases such as PubMed and other indexed repositories.

Future versions could also distinguish:

  • Peer-reviewed studies
  • Preprints
  • Systematic reviews
  • Meta-analyses
  • Clinical guidelines
  • Government publications
  • Educational literature
Evidence Evaluation

A future evidence-analysis layer could evaluate study design, sample size, limitations, risk of bias, and relevance to the research question.

Improved Experiment Reproducibility

Research records could automatically include:

  • Python version
  • Package versions
  • Dataset identifiers
  • Random seeds
  • Model versions
  • Execution timestamps
  • Hardware information
  • Experiment parameters
Stronger Code Isolation

The current source-code filtering could be replaced or supplemented by a genuine sandboxed execution environment with restricted filesystem, network, process, and resource access.

Statistical Validation

Future versions could incorporate dedicated statistical-analysis tools that independently calculate model-performance measures and statistical tests before an LLM is permitted to interpret the results.

EMS Dataset Integration

Structured, de-identified EMS datasets could be incorporated for retrospective research and predictive-model development, subject to appropriate governance and research approval.

Patient Simulation

The existing PatientCase and VitalSigns structures could be expanded into dynamic patient simulations in which physiological observations change in response to simulated interventions.

Human-in-the-Loop Research

Future versions could require researcher approval between major stages:

Hypothesis → Human Review → Experiment → Human Review → Analysis → Human Review → Report

This would provide a stronger safeguard against automated propagation of an incorrect assumption through the entire research pipeline.

Conclusion

Paramedic AI Scientist represents a Python-based prototype for integrating artificial intelligence into an EMS-oriented scientific research workflow.

The application combines literature retrieval, AI-assisted hypothesis generation, experiment selection, Python code generation, controlled computational execution, result analysis, experiment persistence, and automated report generation within a single Streamlit interface.

The system additionally provides structured EMS patient-case representation through PatientCase and VitalSigns, incorporating age, sex, chief complaint, history, physical examination, heart rate, respiratory rate, SpO₂, and ETCO₂.

Its most distinctive feature is the connection between generative AI and executable computational research. The system can move from a natural-language research question through literature review and hypothesis generation to an AI-generated Python experiment, execute that experiment under defined constraints, analyze the output, and incorporate the resulting information into a research report.

This architecture reflects a broader emerging area of research into AI-assisted scientific discovery. Existing literature demonstrates that LLMs can generate potentially useful scientific hypotheses, while also emphasizing the need for validation and human evaluation [1–3].

The application should therefore be understood as a research-assistance and educational prototype, not as an autonomous scientific researcher or clinical decision-making system.

The current implementation demonstrates the feasibility of connecting AI-based reasoning with computational experimentation, but substantial future work is required before such systems could be considered reliable for high-consequence scientific or clinical applications.

Triage & transport decisions

Getting The Right Patient To The Right Hospital, Faster

Deciding whether a patient needs a trauma center, stroke center, or another destination is one of the highest-stakes decisions in prehospital care. Traditional scoring systems can have limitations, which has led researchers to investigate machine-learning approaches that combine multiple patient and operational variables. 1

A 2025 review examined artificial-intelligence approaches to prehospital triage and destination decisions across conditions including trauma, stroke, sepsis, and cardiac presentations. The review reported promising performance from machine-learning models, while also emphasizing the need for validation and implementation research before widespread clinical adoption. 1

Global & low-resource systems

AI May Be Especially Useful Where EMS Resources Are Limited

A 2025 scoping review examined AI applications in prehospital emergency-care systems in low- and middle-income countries. Among the applications identified were demand forecasting, call classification, and disease-risk prediction. 2

These applications are important because EMS performance depends on more than bedside clinical decisions. Knowing where demand is likely to increase can help services think about staffing, dispatch, ambulance availability, and resource allocation.

Demand forecasting

Models can be studied for predicting when and where call volume may increase.

Call classification

AI can help analyze incoming information and support prioritization workflows.

Risk prediction

Research is also exploring models that estimate clinical risk using available patient and system data.

Community-facing tools

AI Support Can Begin Before The Ambulance Arrives

Not every application lives inside the ambulance. Research published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research described an AI-enhanced digital network intended to support prehospital emergency response and community users. 3

This reflects a broader idea: prehospital care can involve callers, bystanders, dispatchers, first responders, EMTs, paramedics, and receiving hospitals. Digital tools may eventually connect more of those steps while keeping trained human professionals in the loop.

Where this goes next

An International Consensus on AI's Future in EMS

A 2026 Delphi consensus study brought together international EMS experts to examine the future role of artificial intelligence in emergency medical services. The study considered domains including communication, clinical care, education, management, operations, and ethics. 4

The important takeaway is not that AI has solved EMS problems. It is that experts are beginning to define where AI may be useful, where evidence is still limited, and where ethical and operational questions remain unresolved. 4

Communication & dispatch

Potential applications include call triage, resource allocation, documentation support, and crew-to-hospital communication.

Clinical decision support

AI may help organize information and identify patterns while leaving clinical decisions with qualified professionals.

Education & training

Adaptive learning, simulation, question generation, and reference tools are potential educational applications.

The important limitation

AI is a Tool — Not Medical Direction

A polished interface can make an AI system look more authoritative than it actually is. That is particularly important in emergency medicine. AI output can be incomplete, incorrect, outdated, or inappropriate for a particular patient.

For that reason, educational AI tools on this site should be used as reference and learning aids. They do not replace local protocols, physician medical direction, certification training, or the judgment of qualified EMS professionals.

For emergencies: Call 911 or use your local emergency number. Do not delay emergency care while consulting an AI system or this website.
